title: Stop Deleting Your PythonAnywhere Files on Every Update. Use Git Instead.
voiceover: I deleted my entire website three times in one month. It always worked. That is exactly why the habit felt safe.

title: Why "delete everything, upload again" eventually blows up
voiceover: Re-uploading everything looks fine, right up to the day you wipe the folder holding your database and your API keys.

title: The mental switch: your server is a copy, not the original
voiceover: The switch is simple. Your laptop writes the code, GitHub holds the truth, and the server just holds a connected copy.

title: Step 1: clone your repo once
voiceover: Clone the repo on the server once, and you finally have the undo button you never had.

title: Step 2: every update after that is one command
voiceover: Every update after that is three commands at home, and one pull on the server.

title: Step 3: reload the web app (the step everybody forgets)
voiceover: Now the step everybody forgets. Pull, then hit Reload, or your site keeps serving the old code from memory.

title: Keep it boring, stay conflict-free
voiceover: One branch, no editing on the server, and your pulls stop conflicting. That is the whole discipline.

title: The whole routine
voiceover: Clone once, pull, reload, and leave the delete button alone. The full walkthrough is on the blog.
bullets: git clone once, to set the project up on PythonAnywhere.
git pull origin main every time you ship updates.
Reload the app from the Web tab.
Stay on a single main branch.
Never edit code on the server. Push from local, pull on the server.
